verses.1:
Al-Mizan presents this sūrah as a Meccan warning to idolaters who reject God and His Messenger: the created world is ordered toward Resurrection and the painful requital of denial, while its arguments also establish Divine Unity and prophethood. The opening Ḥā, Mīm and the Book's descent are treated as previously explained. Creation, terrestrial and supernal, is concomitant with al-ḥaqq and has an inescapable term: at its end this world is annihilated and succeeded by the eternal life of the promised Resurrection. The faithless here are the idolaters who turn from that warning.

Al-Mizan reads the challenge to the gods as an argument that governance cannot be separated from creation. Although the idolaters reserve creation for God, any alleged governor of heaven or earth would need a share in its creation; they must therefore produce an earlier scripture, transmitted knowledge, or vestige of knowledge for that claim. No one is more astray than one who invokes beings that cannot answer at Resurrection and are now oblivious of the invocation; then they will oppose their worshippers and disavow their worship. This wording suggests a degree of life and awareness even in apparently inanimate idols, which will be manifest in the Hereafter. Calling the Qur'an's manifest signs “plain magic” is consequently an evidence-free, arrogant rejection of known truth.

The commentary answers the charge that the Prophet fabricated the Qur'an with two arguments. A fabrication against God would expose him to divine punishment which the idolaters could not avert; and God Himself is sufficient witness that it is His speech, with the Qur'an's challenge to produce its equal establishing that it is divine speech. God being All-forgiving and All-merciful also answers their denial of prophethood: divine wisdom mercifully guides those fit to repent toward forgiveness and eternal happiness, and this requires messengers. The Prophet is not unprecedented in appearance or conduct but human like former messengers, and has neither innate knowledge of nor power over the particular unseen events that will befall him and others. This does not deny Unseen knowledge disclosed through revelation, just as miracles occur only by God's leave; he follows revelation and is a manifest warner.

Al-Mizan then reports abundant narrations from the Imams of the Prophet's Household that God taught the Prophet and the Imams knowledge of all things. It rejects the objection from their ordinary conduct, failures, injuries, and deaths by distinguishing ordinary knowledge (ʿulūm ʿādiyyah) from extraordinary knowledge (ʿulūm ghayr ʿādiyyah). Voluntary acts are possible relative to the will, a component of their sufficient cause (ʿillah tāmmah), yet necessary in objective reality once all causes and conditions obtain; complete knowledge of that reality does not alter its causal sequence. Knowledge alone also need not overcome desire, as obstinate deniers may know their error yet persist. Reports that the Prophet and Imams had special duties, or that ordinary rather than extraordinary knowledge determines duty, can both be reconciled with this account.

On (46:10), the commentary takes the Israelite witness to have testified to the Qur'an's likeness to the original Torah in its divine teachings and then believed; the implicit consequence is that the disdainful idolaters are astray, since God does not guide wrongdoers. Reports identify the witness as the Jewish scholar ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām and support a Medinan revelation; readings that make the testimony a future event, make Moses the witness, or make “its like” mean “the fact of the matter” are rejected as contextually untenable. The faithless' claim that believers could not precede them to a good Qur'an is read as a judgment about believers on account of their faith, not as either proposed alternative grammatical arrangement; their failure of guidance through disdain leads them to call it an ancient fabrication. The prior Torah was an imām and mercy because Israelites followed it and reformed through it, while the Arabic Qur'an confirms it, warns wrongdoers, and gives glad tidings to the virtuous. Finally, affirming that God alone is Lord and remaining steadfast (istaqāmū) by meeting the confession's practical demands removes fear of future punishment and grief over punishment suffered; such people are abiding companions (aṣḥāb) of Paradise, rewarded for their obedience and sacrifice.

verses.3: Al-Mizan takes the heavens, earth, and what lies between them to be the perceptible terrestrial and supernal world. Creation is concomitant with al-ḥaqq and has a specified, unexceedable term: the universe will be annihilated, then followed by the eternal world of the promised Resurrection. The faithless are the idolaters, and their disregard concerns the warning of Judgment and its painful punishment for associating partners with God.
verses.4: Al-Mizan reads “Do you see?” and “Show me” as demands to be informed about the idols invoked besides God. Though the plural used for them reflects the idolaters' attribution of intelligent action, the argument applies to every alleged deity: one who shares cosmic governance must share creation, for governance without creation is meaningless. Since the idolaters themselves ascribe creation to God, they must produce an earlier divine scripture, transmitted knowledge, or a vestige of knowledge proving that their gods share in creating heaven or earth. The commentary takes athārah, “trace,” primarily as transmitted knowledge, while noting the closely related reading of a vestige.
verses.5: Al-Mizan treats the question as declaring that no one is more astray than the worshipper of beings unable to answer until the Day of Resurrection, when this world to which the invocations are confined has ended. Their present obliviousness is additional to their inability to benefit worshippers; it prepares for their future enmity and disavowal of that worship. Because “oblivious” properly describes something capable of sensing, the commentary infers that life and awareness in some degree inhere even in stone and wooden idols.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains ḥashr as people being forcibly brought from their graves to the Resurrection gathering. Their own gods will then become enemies and disavow their idolatrous worship. The commentary understands the reported speech of such objects to show that things apparently lifeless in this world, including idols, will be shown alive in the Hereafter.
verses.7: Al-Mizan reads the verse and the next as a rebuke: the “manifest signs” are Qur'anic verses, expressly substituted by “the truth” to show what has come to them. The faithless cannot reasonably call known, manifest truth “plain magic”; they reject it without evidence and out of arrogance.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan takes the opening particle to mean, “Rather, they say” that he fabricated the Qur'an. The conditional answer is deliberately implicit: had the Prophet fabricated speech against God, God would seize and punish him, and the idolaters could not protect him, so he has no reason to expose himself to that certain punishment for their sake. God knows their idle talk—whether about the Qur'an or their denials of sorcery and fabrication—and is a second, sufficient witness that it is His speech; the Qur'an's challenge to produce its equal establishes that it is divine speech.

The commentary reads the two divine names as also refuting their denial of prophethood. God's forgiveness and mercy, required by His wisdom, guide those who turn to Him and are worthy of nearness, forgiveness, and eternal happiness. That guidance is bestowed through prophetic missions, so divine wisdom requires a messenger to lead them to it.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan prefers the reading that the Prophet is not a novelty because he does not differ from former messengers in appearance, conduct, speech, or deed: he is a human subject to their human frailties, answering those who objected to a messenger who ate and walked in marketplaces. “I do not know what will be done with me or with you” denies innate knowledge of particular unseen events and any power over what the unseen brings; God alone does what He wills. It does not deny Unseen knowledge disclosed through revelation, nor miracles performed solely by God's leave. The continuation, “I follow what is revealed to me,” marks precisely that contrast, and “a manifest warner” confirms the whole account.

Al-Mizan reports abundant narrations from the Imams of the Prophet's Household that God taught the Prophet and the Imams knowledge of all things, with the Prophet's knowledge received through revelation and the Imams' returning to him. It rejects the objection that their ordinary conduct, reverses, injuries, and deaths would have been impossible had they known the unseen. The objection confuses ordinary knowledge (ʿulūm ʿādiyyah) with extraordinary knowledge (ʿulūm ghayr ʿādiyyah), which knows reality but does not change worldly events.

Voluntary acts depend on will and other material, temporal, and spatial conditions. When these jointly form the sufficient cause (ʿillah tāmmah), the act necessarily occurs; relative to the will, one component of that cause, it remains possible. Thus every phenomenon, including voluntary action, is necessary in the objective causal order, and complete certainty of reality cannot alter a link in that order. Nor does knowing one is wrong necessarily redirect desire: obstinate disbelievers may be certain yet persist, and knowledge without the soul's resolve does not produce action. Al-Mizan says the reported answers that the Prophet and Imams had special duties, or that their duty is determined by ordinary rather than extraordinary knowledge, are compatible with this analysis.
verses.10: Al-Mizan takes the pronouns to refer to the Qur'an and “its like” to mean its likeness to the original Torah in divine teachings. The Israelite witness testifies to that likeness and believes, while the idolaters disdain belief; the omitted consequence is therefore that they are astray, for God does not guide wrongdoing people, rather than merely that they are wrongdoers. Reports identify the witness as the Jewish scholar ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām, supporting a Medinan revelation. The commentary rejects a future-event reading because it cannot argue with idolaters who deny the Prophet, rejects Moses as witness because no proof requires the verse to be Meccan and that reading makes Moses an irrelevant standard for them, and finds the “fact of the matter” meaning of likeness equally unlikely.
verses.11: Al-Mizan reads the faithless as saying about the believers, on account of their belief, that if belief in the Qur'an were good the believers would not have preceded them to it. It rejects readings that divide “the faithful” and “they” between separate groups or treat the wording as a shift of address. Since their own disdain prevents guidance through the Qur'an, they call it an ancient fabrication, like their claim that its message is myths of the ancients.
verses.12: Al-Mizan reads “Yet before it” as qualifying the accusation of an ancient lie: the Torah preceded the Qur'an as a guide and mercy, and the Arabic Qur'an confirms it while warning wrongdoers and bringing glad tidings to the virtuous. The Torah is an imām because Israelites followed it in daily life, and a mercy for believers who followed it to reform themselves.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains “Our Lord is God” as affirming that lordship belongs to God alone, and istaqāmū as holding to that testimony without deviation while fulfilling its practical demands. Their promised freedom from fear concerns no future harm or punishment, and freedom from grief concerns no punishment or terror already suffered. The wording makes this the consequence for whoever makes the confession and remains steadfast.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains that the righteous are called companions (aṣḥāb) of Paradise because they will stay with it, and “remaining in it” emphatically confirms that they never leave. Their eternal residence recompenses their worldly obedience and sacrifice.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan reads God's injunction to man as an injunction to an action concerning parents, namely kindness; the alternative grammatical analyses of iḥsānan all converge on that sense. Kindness and dutifulness to parents have been ordained across religious traditions. The mother's hardship in carrying, bearing, and weaning her child both explains the wisdom of the command and awakens empathy. Thirty months combines the shortest pregnancy, six months, with the two years of nursing; forty is ordinarily the maturity of intellect.

The prayer asks God to inspire (īzāʿ), not with previously unknown knowledge but with the inner motivation to thank Him and act righteously. Blessing (niʿmah) includes outward gifts such as life and sustenance and inward gifts such as faith and reliance. Verbal thanksgiving praises God, while practical thanksgiving uses gifts as God's gifts and manifests servanthood (ʿubūdiyyah). The speaker gives thanks for blessings granted to himself and his parents, remembering and praying for them, asks for deeds pleasing to God, and asks that his descendants be made righteous, which will benefit him through their dutifulness to him.

Al-Mizan says the prayer's core is purity of soul and righteous conduct. Repentance and submission mean surrendering the matter to God and desiring only what He desires; because God confirms this prayer by promising acceptance in the next verse, their conjunction leads to purified hearts (mukhlaṣīn dhātan) and actions wholly dedicated to God (mukhliṣīn ʿamalan). No act is acceptable or raised to Him unless it is done purely for His sake.
verses.16: Al-Mizan says taqabbal conveys more than mere approval: God accepts the best of their deeds, namely obedient obligatory and supererogatory acts. Morally neutral acts (mubāḥāt), even if good, are not included in acceptance, as the contrast with overlooking misdeeds confirms. “Among the inhabitants of Paradise” qualifies those whose misdeeds are overlooked. This is a true promise previously conveyed through prophets and messengers, or a true promise for Judgment given through this acceptance and pardon.
verses.17: Al-Mizan contrasts the penitent, submissive believer of the preceding verse with one who disbelieves in God, His Messenger, and Resurrection, and angrily reviles his parents for warning him. His question about being brought forth after generations have passed denies resurrection on the mistaken premise that the dead should already have returned in this world; the promised resurrection is instead in the Hereafter, a new creation. His parents invoke God's aid as they call him to believe in God, the Messenger, and what the Messenger brings, warning that God's promise is true. He dismisses either that promise or the whole religion as myths of the earliest nations. Though grammatically singular, this person is plural in meaning, and the predicate identifying those against whom the word is due comes in (46:18).
verses.18: Al-Mizan identifies these people as those against whom the divine word has become due alongside prior nations of jinn and humans, and declares them losers. It refers readers to its earlier discussion of the expression.
verses.19: Al-Mizan says both virtuous believers and vicious disbelievers have distinct ascending and descending stations: Paradise has darajāt and hell darakāt. These degrees arise from differences in their souls, though manifested through deeds, so the degrees belong to them while their source is their actions. Recompensing them fully means giving them their deeds in another form, indicating tajassum al-aʿmāl, the physical reality of deeds in the Hereafter; a reported alternative understands it as giving the wages of their works. In either case, they are not wronged.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan rejects both the claim that being “offered” the Fire merely means being punished in it and the proposed inversion that the Fire was really offered to the faithless. The former makes the later command to taste punishment redundant, while the latter wrongly assumes the offered-to must perceive the offering and that hell has no senses. The commentary cites authentic narrations that Paradise and hell have senses and Qur'anic speech by hell, and it also rejects the requirement that the offering move toward the offered-to.

“Offering” (ʿaraḍ) signifies a relation (nisbah) in which either party may be the principal offered-to (maʿrūḍ ʿalayh) and the other the ancillary offering (maʿrūḍ). Hell can be offered to the faithless, showing that no good deed or intercession prevents their entry; conversely, the faithless can be offered to hell, showing nothing prevents it from punishing them. Al-Mizan therefore considers two offerings most likely: hell comes into view before the faithless, then, after weighing and judgment, they are offered to it as they are driven into it.

Their “good things” are what accords with the soul (nafs) and nature (ṭabʿ). They exhausted them by receiving them in full and enjoying them for their own sake rather than to prepare for the Hereafter, leaving nothing to enjoy there. The humiliating punishment consequently answers two sins: undue disdain for truth in belief, and transgression in action.
verses.21: Al-Mizan identifies the brother of ʿĀd as the Prophet Hūd, related to his people through his father. Aḥqāf lay certainly in the southern Arabian Peninsula, though its exact location is disputed and no trace remains. “Warners” means messengers here, not also scholars as their deputies; the preferred reading takes “in front of him and behind him” to mean that Hūd warned them after a gap in messengers. His prohibition of worshipping anyone but God states the foundation to which all religion returns, Divine Unity. The “tremendous day” apparently means their worldly annihilation rather than Resurrection, as their subsequent demand to hasten the threatened punishment and the reply at (46:24) show.
verses.22: Al-Mizan explains taʾfikanā as derived from a root of falsehood and calumny but used here for turning aside. Hūd's people accuse him of trying falsely and slanderously to divert them from their gods, then demand the threatened punishment to expose him, in their view, as a fraud and liar.
verses.23: Al-Mizan reads Hūd's reply as limiting knowledge of the punishment's nature, mode, and time to God, because it belongs to the Unseen. Hūd only communicates what he was sent with and has no power to satisfy their demand. Calling them senseless means that, by rejecting God's call and signs and mocking the warning, they cannot distinguish benefit from harm or good from evil.
verses.24: Al-Mizan explains that ʿĀd saw the approaching ʿāriḍ, a horizon cloud that spreads across the sky, and rejoiced in the expectation of rain. The correction, “Rather,” derides their demand to hasten punishment and discloses the cloud's reality: a hurricane carrying painful punishment; the speaker is God, though some attribute the words to Hūd. Its destruction of “everything” is limited by context to people, animals, and property rather than the land itself, leaving only dwellings visible. The concluding statement generalizes this exemplary severity as God's way of requiting the guilty.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains that ʿĀd saw the approaching ʿāriḍ, a horizon cloud that spreads across the sky, and rejoiced in the expectation of rain. The correction, “Rather,” derides their demand to hasten punishment and discloses the cloud's reality: a hurricane carrying painful punishment; the speaker is God, though some attribute the words to Hūd. Its destruction of “everything” is limited by context to people, animals, and property rather than the land itself, leaving only dwellings visible. The concluding statement generalizes this exemplary severity as God's way of requiting the guilty.
verses.26: Al-Mizan draws from ʿĀd an admonition to Meccan disbelievers: God had granted them greater physical strength, vigor, and power, as well as hearing, sight, and hearts to apprehend benefit and harm and distinguish between them. Yet these faculties could not protect them when they stubbornly impugned God's signs; those who likewise deny the signs have no reason to feel secure from punishment. The commentary records the alternative that these faculties were given to hear truth, see signs of Divine Unity, and infer an Origin and Destination, but judges its first reading more suited to the context. It also notes that samʿ is singular in form but plural in sense because it originally functions as a verbal noun. What they derided ultimately besieged them.
verses.27: Al-Mizan treats the destruction of surrounding towns as a warning joined to the preceding admonition, rather than directly to Hūd's account. God varied signs—prophetic miracles, revelation, blessings, and trials by hardship—so their inhabitants might take warning, repent, abandon wrongdoing, and return to worshipping God alone. “They” refers to the inhabitants of the towns.
verses.28: Al-Mizan reads the question as derision: the inhabitants had taken false gods, besides God, in order to seek nearness to Him, yet those gods gave no help. Their forsaking them shows the collapse and falsity of the claimed bond of lordship (rubūbiyyah) and servanthood (ʿubūdiyyah) on which they expected rescue. “That was their lie and what they fabricated” primarily means that their gods' forsaking them resulted from their lie and fabrication. Alternatively, it can refer to their destruction together with that forsaking as the reality disproving their fabricated claim that the gods would intercede and bring them near to God; this too is derisive.
verses.29: Al-Mizan reads ṣarf as directing or moving a group and nafar, following Rāghib, as a small group of at least three, applicable to humans or jinn. The jinn attended the Qur’an in its active sense, its recitation, told one another to be silent so as to listen, and, when the recitation ended, departed to warn their people of God’s punishment.
verses.30: Al-Mizan identifies the Book heard by the jinn as the Qur’an, which appears to indicate that they believed in Moses and his scripture. Its confirmation covers either the Torah or all heavenly scriptures, and it guides followers to truth and a straight path from which beliefs and conduct do not stray.
verses.31: Al-Mizan says that God’s summoner is the Prophet, not the Qur’an. It reads min in forgiveness as tabʿīḍ: faith remits the sins earned before belief, as in (8:38). The alternative which limits forgiveness to God’s rights rather than rights owed to people is rejected because Islam effaces what came before it.
verses.32: Al-Mizan explains that rejecting God’s summoner cannot thwart God or impair His plan; even the help of others cannot protect the rejecter. Refusal harms only the person who refuses, which is why the verse concludes that such people are in manifest error.
verses.33: Al-Mizan reads “see” as insight and takes “exhausted” more eloquently to mean rendered impotent rather than tired. Since God created the heavens and earth and originates all existence and life without impotence, He is able to revive the dead; bi qādirin’s added bāʾ follows the negative question, “Is not God able…?”
verses.34: Al-Mizan holds that the foretold exposure of Resurrection-deniers to the Fire affirms the preceding argument: their admission that it is a fact will be followed by punishment for their disbelief.
verses.35: Al-Mizan treats the command as a consequence of the demonstrated and foretold Resurrection: the Prophet must endure deniers as the Resolute Messengers (rusul ūlū al-ʿazm) did and not seek their punishment, since it will surely reach them. When they see it, their worldly life will seem only an hour, showing its nearness. The Qur’an and its explanation are a prophetic proclamation; only transgressors who abandon servanthood are destroyed. Although ʿazm has been read as patience, fidelity to the prophets’ pledge, or resolution denoting governance (ḥukm) and law (sharīʿah), the narrations of the Imāms of the Prophet’s Household make the last correct: the five are Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad (42:13). Al-Mizan rejects the numerous other enumerations as unsupported or reliant on proofs that do not establish them.
